sections.content: You know the *pretérito perfecto* from Unit 1: *haber* + past participle. Some time words go with it because they name a time that has not finished yet: *hoy* (today), *esta mañana* (this morning) and *esta tarde* (this afternoon). You know *hoy* and *esta tarde* from A1; now they come with the *pretérito perfecto*. In Spain, the *pretérito perfecto* is the normal past for things that happened today; for yesterday and earlier you will learn another past tense in Unit 11.

items.english: Today we have arrived at the pier.

items.spanish: Esta mañana hemos visto las cuevas.
items.english: This morning we have seen the caves.

items.spanish: Esta tarde la barquera ha remado despacio.
items.english: This afternoon the boatwoman has rowed slowly.

items.spanish: Hoy Carlos ha visto el río.
items.english: Today Carlos has seen the river.

sections.content: Think of a time that is still going on: today is not over, so the *pretérito perfecto* fits. Put the time word first, then *he / has / ha / hemos / han* + the participle.
